verdict: Avoid new refining-linked exposure in Numaligarh; the data call is Avoid and the news flow is worse, so lend only to downstream service and logistics borrowers with contracted cash flows, and decline refinery-dependent SMEs.
title: Numaligarh Petroleum Refining & Coal Products: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
A refinery buys crude, runs it through distillation and secondary units, and sells LPG, petrol, diesel, naphtha and petrochemical feedstock. Cash comes in daily at the pump and gate; cash goes out on crude purchase terms and on power, catalyst and maintenance. **Value sits in the crude-to-product spread (GRM), not in volume, so a borrower's cash flow moves with Brent and with the product crack, not with how busy the plant looks.** Numaligarh Refinery processed over three thousand 113 Thousand Metric Tonnes of crude in FY2025-26 at 103% utilisation, beyond its rated 3 MMTPA for the second year, with LPG output up over 22% in March 2026 alone [3]. That is the anchor plant; everything else in this city is a supplier, contractor or servicer to it.

## Where cash and risk sit now
**The macro numbers have turned against the sector.** India-wide IIP for NIC 19 output is -0.6% YoY and -0.9% Apr-to-date [D], and Brent at $113/bbl is above the $75-100 band [D]. High crude with falling output squeezes working capital: the same tonne of throughput now ties up more cash in inventory and receivables. **Assam's own demand signal is weak: electricity demand is +1.9% Apr-to-date versus India's +9.5%, 7.6 pp slower [D].** Read that as a local activity brake, so when a proposal lands, check the borrower's monthly sales to non-refinery customers; if that line is flat or falling, ask what share of revenue depends on the plant's own expansion spend.

## What peers and ratings say
Peer results are strong but margin-led, not volume-led: HPCL's GRM rose to US$32.2/bbl (+35% QoQ, +262% YoY) on throughput down 6% YoY [7], and BPCL's Q2 beat came as Brent moved from around $70/bbl in mid-July [4]. IOC reports domestic under-recovery of INR 184 per cylinder in September, INR 229 in October, projected at INR 309 in November and INR 370 in December [6]. **That under-recovery path is the single most useful number for us: it tells you the marketing side is absorbing cost, so refinery-linked receivables will stretch before they break.** ICRA's Stable outlook on HPCL/HMEL rests on adequate cash generation over 12-18 months [8]; CPCL's rating flags fossil-fuel transition as a distant risk only [9]. Note [11] is from 2017 and should not be used.

## Who to pursue and how to grow safely
**Pursue the plant's service tail, not its shadow: transport contractors with signed freight agreements, catalyst and chemical suppliers with purchase orders, and LPG cylinder logistics with monthly billing to the refinery.** Avoid traders who buy and resell product on price speculation, and avoid any SME whose receivable is a single refinery bill with no written terms. Structure as a cash-flow loan against assigned receivables, keep tenor inside the contract, and take a monthly stock-and-debtor statement plus bank statement. **Take the GRM and under-recovery print every month alongside the borrower's own billing, because the borrower's cash arrives after the refinery's margin is decided.**

## Early-warning signs
- Monthly receivable days from the refinery (monthly): if days stretch beyond the contract term, stop fresh disbursement and re-price.
- Brent above $100/bbl (weekly): if sustained, cut limits on borrowers with no pass-through clause.
- Assam electricity demand growth (monthly, CEA): if it stays below India's rate, defer new capex-linked lending.
- Refinery throughput and utilisation (quarterly): if utilisation drops below rated capacity, ask for revised cash-flow projections.
- IOC under-recovery per cylinder (monthly): if it keeps rising, expect slower payments down the chain.
